title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation
authors: Samarth Sarin, Lovepreet Singh, Dhagash Mehta
abstract: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. title: ChildAI-Gov: An Evidence-Linked AI System for Assessing EdTech Policies Against Children's Digital Rights
authors: Naveen Sigalapalli, Huizhi Liang, Clara Crivellaro
abstract: We present ChildAI-Gov, an explainable AI system for assessing whether education-technology (EdTech) policies respect children's digital rights. Generative AI is reaching children's education faster than its governance can keep pace, yet checking a tool against children's rights remains manual, expert-dependent, and slow. We propose the Child Rights Impact Score (CRIS), an evidence-linked measure across five dimensions: safety, privacy, transparency, autonomy, and non-discrimination. ChildAI-Gov

title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
authors: Ali Yousefi, Nikos Komninos, Hafizul Asad
abstract: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctn

title: Explicit Style Extraction for Personalized Long-Form Text Generation
authors: Jenitha Reddy Patel, Sameeksha Kini, Amulya Rayasam et al.
abstract: Personalized long-form generation asks a language model to write new text the way a specific user would. The standard recipe, retrieval-augmented generation, places a few of the user's past texts in the prompt but leaves the model to decide what to take from them. We introduce StylePrism, a taxonomy of 28 stylistic aspects in seven categories, and SP-Refine, an inference-time method that makes style extraction an explicit step: the model first fills StylePrism with the user's patterns, quoted ev

title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT
authors: Maximilian Rokuss, Jeya Maria Jose Valanarasu, Alejandro Lozano et al.
abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. title: Potential emergence in LLM agents: a statistical physics perspective
authors: Zhuo-Yang Song, Hua Xing Zhu
abstract: There has been significant recent interest in understanding the behaviour of LLM agents from the perspective of human preferences or corpus statistics. In this paper we propose agent states as intermediate variables through which post-training can be measured and predicted. From a statistical physics perspective, we study the emergence of a global potential which governs the transition of state in LLM agent reasoning. We introduce a partition function to model the ideal KL-regularised transition

title: Bringing AI Assistance to the Beznau Nuclear Power Plant: A Hierarchical System of LLM Agents for Reactor Monitoring
authors: Wenqi Zhou, Leonardo Baldo, Edwin Kolbe et al.
abstract: Beznau Unit 1 in Switzerland, in operation since 1969, is the most experienced nuclear reactor still running worldwide. Five decades of incremental modernization have left its monitoring systems, alarm logs, variable catalogs, technical specifications and investigation reports in separate silos that were never designed to be queried together. As a result, investigating a core instrumentation anomaly means slow, manual gathering of knowledge scattered across databases, documents, and experienced

title: Fix Where It Fails: Root-Cause-Guided Agentic Harness Optimization for Scene Graph Generation
authors: Jee Eun Kim, Donghyeon Choi, Sangjune An et al.
abstract: Scene graph generation (SGG) aims to detect objects in an image and predict the relationships between them. The standard PredCls, SGCls, and SGDet settings show how much performance drops without ground-truth boxes and labels, but not where or why a model fails. Knowing this would allow fixing a model where it fails, without retraining. We propose RoHa-SGG (Root-cause-guided Harness optimization for SGG), which extends agentic harness optimization to SGG. It optimizes the harness, the inference

title: From Manufacturing Event Logs to Simulation: Enabling SMEs with Agentic AI for SimPy Simulation Generation
authors: Richard Reider, Lina Döring, Sebastian Lang et al.
abstract: High expertise and cost barriers exclude small and medium-sized enterprises from discrete-event simulation (DES). We introduce GenAI4SimPy, a multi-agent framework powered by Qwen 3.6 (27B), an open-weight large language model, that automates end-to-end DES generation from manufacturing event logs to executable SimPy models through tool-augmented reasoning and human-in-the-loop validation. Evaluated on three execution blocks from a public smart factory dataset, the framework achieved a mean abso

title: Belief-State Management Meets Rubric Rewards for Agentic Forecasting
authors: Jingyi Chai, Yun Liao, Hao Lu et al.
abstract: Current large language model (LLM) agents still struggle to forecast real-world events. This stems from two primary limitations: i) standard ReAct harness accumulates reasoning and evidence within one growing context, and ii) outcome-based rewards in forecasting lead to a slow and noisy signal that cannot distinguish sound reasoning from lucky guesses. title: Correct Precedents Induce Policy Violations in On-Device LLM Agents
authors: Chong Tian, Yu Wang, Steve Liu et al.
abstract: Local-cloud agent systems pair a cloud model with a small on-device agent that acts on private data, often as the last check before an irreversible action. We identify, for the first time, a failure in which such an agent is led into a violation by its own correct decisions within a session. After it correctly releases an item whose restriction was lifted, it becomes more likely to release the next item that is still restricted. Because the trigger is a correct decision, a history with no faulty

title: Do Senior Agents Do Their Job? Measuring Role Integrity in How LLM Agents Use Subordinate Material
authors: Jinxiang Xie, Xinyi Zhang, Changjiang Jiang et al.
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly divide long tasks among subagents whose reports a senior agent turns into the final answer. Such a division of labor pays off only if each agent, and above all the senior agent, carries out the duties of its role. Current evaluations, however, mostly score the final answer, and a fluent, well-cited answer cannot show whether the senior agent weighed its subagents' reports or merely aggregated them. To assess whether a senior agent meets its assigned responsib

title: CoEvoBench: Can LLMs Drive Recursive Co-Evolution of Agentic Systems?
authors: Chuan Xiao, Baojie Wang, Haizhao Fan et al.
abstract: The performance of an LLM agent depends on both its model and its harness, the code that mediates its interaction with tools and environments. Can LLM researchers drive this co-evolution as a recursive improvement process, deciding round after round which component to change when each change alters the value of the other? Existing benchmarks evaluate post-training or data research with the harness out of scope, or harness optimization with the model fixed, leaving this joint decision unmeasured.

title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
authors: Sean Maxwell
abstract: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. title: Separating Automation Gains from Agent Contributions in AI-Assisted Model Validation
authors: M. Ahmadi Achachlouei
abstract: LLM agents are being proposed for bank model validation, yet evaluations that compare agent-assisted work with manual practice credit the agent with gains that come from digitized evidence and deterministic tests. We propose a staged architecture in which an LLM-free controlled workflow (P1) is both the fallback and the control arm for individually authorized agent tasks (P2), and an attribution protocol that credits an agent only for faults P1 does not already report. The protocol charges decoy

title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
authors: Raphaël Bonnet-Guerrini, Johann Ioannou-Nikolaides, Troels Petersen
abstract: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: Stateful Privacy Sniffing of LLM Agents via Behavioral Covert Channels in Web Interactions
authors: Ruichao Liang, Wenzhong Deng, Jing Chen et al.
abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on Web interaction, issuing searches, following links, and reading pages, to complete complex user tasks. Since each action is driven by the agent's private context, including the user's prompt, dialogue history, memory, and connected data, it also opens a new privacy exposure surface. title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
authors: Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang et al.
abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. title: SecretAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Privacy Protection against Vision Language Models
authors: Minda Zhao, Yue Zhang, Mengyu Wang
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against

title: Learning When to Ask: Advisor-Aware Post-Training for SLM Agents
authors: Aasheesh Singh, Vishal Vaddina
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. title: From Letter-of-Credit Requirements to Executable Specifications: Evaluating Verification Accuracy and Completeness
authors: Ji Sub Choi, Whan Choi, Seo Yeon Gu et al.
abstract: In letter-of-credit (LC) document examination, a correct final decision does not show that every requirement was examined. We therefore evaluate examination requirement by requirement and make each requirement executable. title: Keep the Process, Change the Supplier: Runtime Governance for Tool-Using AI Agents
authors: Deepak Waghmare, Shaad Sufi
abstract: Tool-using AI agents propose actions whose authorization and external effects cannot be inferred from generated text alone. We study an execution boundary that separates agent proposals from business-controlled authority, context disclosure, and supplier selection. The Open Process Control Plane (OPCP) mediates capability calls and records uncertain outcomes when a supplier may have acted without returning an acceptable reply. We evaluate this runtime with scripted requests and synthetic supplie

title: SLP-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Acoustic Claims of Reasoning Audio Language Models on Clinical Speech
authors: Côme Hosxe, Rachid Riad, Quentin Spinat
abstract: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Be

title: Evaluating Prompting Strategies for Zero-Shot Multilingual Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis with Large Language Models
authors: Jakub Šm{í}d, Pavel Kr{á}l
abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have advanced natural language understanding, their ability to perform complex target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD) -- a key task within aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) -- in zero-shot multilingual settings remains underexplored. title: Abstract What Varies, Reuse Longer Patterns: Efficient Offline Chain-of-Thought Compression
authors: Shibo Wang, Yuzhe He, Yifeng Zhao et al.
abstract: Offline chain-of-thought (CoT) compression creates shorter supervision for efficient reasoning, but per-example compressors repeatedly process similar expressions across traces, wasting compressor budget. Methods that reuse identical text across examples miss longer shared expressions when names, numbers, or formulas change from one question to another. title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
authors: Feng Huang, Qiang Huang, Yue Gao et al.
abstract: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
authors: Ahaan Dabholkar, Harshvardhan Patel, Michalis Polychronakis et al.
abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. title: Reasoning in Fewer Tokens: Concept-Normalized Multilingual Scratchpads and Reversible Model-Adaptive Reasoning Codes
authors: Rabimba Karanjai, Suryabhan Singh Hada, Hemanth Hegadehalli Madhavarao et al.
abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting significantly improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) but incurs high inference costs due to lengthy autoregressive decoding. While previous efficiency approaches reduce costs by discarding tokens or utilizing continuous latent representations, these lossy methods fundamentally sacrifice interpretability and auditability. In this work, we introduce a novel compression framework for intermediate reasoning. We apply Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to

title: Do Language Models Know Which Words Steer Their Reasoning?
authors: Yanbei Jiang, Chao Lei, Jey Han Lau et al.
abstract: While chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps from language models, it is unclear which words in the context actually steer the CoT. We identify Phantom Context Influence (PCI): language models are disproportionately steered by semantically irrelevant context words, even as the same models deny those words' relevance when asked. title: Can Reasoning and Image Description Enhance Yes/No Visual Mathematical Understanding?
authors: Guangcheng Song, Weichuan Wang, Linqi Song
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general visual tasks, yet their ability to understand mathematical images remains limited. This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs' performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Though

title: Learning Adaptive Defense Strategies: Fine-Tuned LLMs for Network Security Games under Network Mobility
authors: Md Abu Sayed, Asif Rahman, Ahmed Ryen et al.
abstract: Large language models(LLM) show promise for strategic reasoning, yet their ability to compute game-theoretic equilibria under dynamic conditions remains largely unexplored. This work investigates whether fine-tuned LLMs can serve as solver-free surrogates for online equilibrium computation in honeypot allocation, a setting in which network mobility continuously reshapes the underlying attack graph and forces repeated re-solving of a two-player zero-sum game. title: Reasoning in Two Dimensions: Quantifying Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness and Efficiency
authors: Chenruo Liu, Quan Zhang, Qi Lei
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning exposes intermediate steps, but a correct answer does not establish that an LLM relies on the dependence expressed by those steps or reasons efficiently. We operationalize CoT faithfulness and efficiency within a common framework. title: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search
authors: Yi Ding, Gaurav Kumar, Rui Min et al.
abstract: Sustaining user experience (UX) quality in large-scale web search requires scalable evaluation. Traditional surveys are slow and bottleneck rapid A/B testing, while automated metrics often lack the granularity to diagnose visual-spatial UX anomalies. To address this, we introduce the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework, a novel industrial architecture for automated UX attribution. title: RoSci: Exploring Robustness in Science VLMs
authors: Junying Wang, Yijin Guo, Yalun Wu et al.
abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable significant progress in scientific tasks. However, these models are generally assumed to be presented with complete and accurate information, overlooking the challenges of erroneous/missing information in wild scenarios. title: Can Vision-Language Models Synthesize Executable Game-Playing Programs?
authors: Yao Tong, Jiaxin Qi, Dingyu Zhang et al.
abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have endowed multimodal agents with increasingly strong visual perception and long-horizon reasoning capabilities, making VLM-based autonomous game playing feasible. Existing game benchmarks primarily evaluate whether an agent can select appropriate actions from the current visual state across different scenarios and games. title: ORBIT: Offset-based Activation Steering for Cross-lingual Multimodal Fact Verification
authors: Huy Trieu, Duy-Minh Nguyen-Tran, Thanh-Dat Nguyen et al.
abstract: Multimodal fact verification faces a fundamental accessibility bottleneck: while large proprietary models exhibit cross-lingual robustness, small vision-language models suffer a severe, disproportionate accuracy collapse on low-resource languages. Closing this gap traditionally requires prohibitive scale or extensive language-specific fine-tuning. title: Unimodal Shortcuts and Joint Scene-Intent Dependence in Vision-Language Safety Representations
authors: Guijia Zhang, Hongbo Qiu, Guohao Cai et al.
abstract: The safety of a request to a vision-language model often depends on the image: asking how to serve a dish is harmless for fresh food and harmful for spoiled food. High accuracy on situational safety benchmarks does not tell us whether a model's safety representation encodes both the scene and the user's intent, because a benchmark can often be solved from one modality alone. title: EAGLE: Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding
authors: Zhongjian Zou, Quan Qian
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with fine-grained understanding of high-resolution images: attention heads vary in their reliability for grounding target entities and their attributes, while localized details are often disconnected from the broader scene context. We propose EAGLE (Entity-Aware Grounding with Layered Evidence for High-Resolution Image Understanding), a plug-in framework that jointly selects grounding signals and organizes hierarchical visual evidence. EAGL

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Qwen3-VL for Handwritten Mathematical Expression Recognition
authors: Manh Tuan Ha, Xuan Bao Viet Tran, Vo Minh Dat Nguyen et al.
abstract: Handwritten mathematical expression recognition (HMER) requires joint recovery of symbol identity and two-dimensional syntax, so a locally plausible transcription may still be structurally wrong. We study whether a compact vision-language model can be adapted to generate linearized Symbol Label Graphs (SLGs) under limited computing resources. title: Dynamic Token Merging for Efficient Vision-Language Models
authors: Chris Gu, Marco Andono Sie, Nathan Zhou et al.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) represent each image with hundreds of visual tokens, which can make inference costly even when a prompt depends on only part of the image. Dynamic Token Merging (DTM), introduced in MrT5 for byte-level text encoders, learns which tokens to remove: a lightweight delete gate scores contextualized hidden states, acts as a differentiable attention bias during training, and physically removes tokens at inference. title: When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models
authors: Yao Tong, Jiaxin Qi, Yan Cui et al.
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. title: What Does the Visual Encoder Buy? Visual Information Gain in Encoder-Free Multimodal Pretraining
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Anqi Li, Wei Qiu
abstract: Recent scaling studies ask whether vision-language models still need a visual encoder by comparing encoder-free and encoder-based models on the next-token loss of the text in image-text data. This loss can fall without any use of the image, and two runs with the same loss can differ in what they take from it. title: Structurally Different, Functionally Persistent: Capability Regions Under Model Optimization
authors: Jiwoo Kum, Chanwoo Kim, Doyun Kim et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) capabilities have been associated with localized parameter regions, enabling targeted model editing and intervention. However, it remains unclear whether a region identified before model optimization remains an effective intervention target afterward. We evaluate the functional persistence and parameter overlap of coding capability regions across three instruction-tuned models under quantization, pruning, and LoRA-based adaptation. title: HR-Merge: Model Merging with Headroom-Weighted Residual Refinement
authors: Jiakang Huang, Xueyan Zhang, Renyi Cai et al.
abstract: Model merging combines experts fine-tuned from a shared backbone, such as LoRA adapters of a large language model, into one multi-task model without further training. Existing methods apply one rule to every task, yet the accuracy they lose is uneven across tasks. title: Composable Soft-Prompt Distillation of RL Experts: Toward Continual Post-Training
authors: Zhen Zhang, Changyi Yang, Xuehai He et al.
abstract: RL post-training typically produces domain experts that must then be consolidated into one model, and as new experts keep arriving, this consolidation becomes a continual process. Weight merging and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) must re-consolidate the whole model whenever an expert is added, and can erode capabilities outside the target domains. title: Structure Over Scale: Rethinking Adaptation for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
authors: Allan Kazakov, Abdurrahman Javat
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is often framed as a choice between the expressivity of Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) and the efficiency of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We find that this framing misses an important variable: the geometry of the update. Under a common cold-start GRPO protocol, LoRA exhibits rank collapse: performance remains broadly stable at low rank, then fails abruptly as rank increases. title: How Does SAM-3 Adapt? Capacity, Update Geometry, and Domain Transfer
authors: Allan Kazakov, Abdurrahman Javat, Duygu Cakir
abstract: Promptable segmentation foundation models are increasingly used in specialized domains, but it remains unclear how SAM-3 should be fine-tuned when adapting it beyond its original training distribution. We study this question by comparing five adaptation families --LoRA, HiRA, KRAdapter, QuanTA, and Full Fine-Tuning-- across five segmentation datasets spanning medical imaging, remote sensing, and dense material segmentation. title: Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation
authors: Yalin Yang, Xiao Huang, Yanan Wu et al.
abstract: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. title: The Assistant Persona Differs Across Languages in Activation Space
authors: Daniel Yoo, Naama Rozen, Evan Harris
abstract: Large language models behave differently across languages, and are noticeably less safe in lower-resource languages. This gap is well established behaviorally, but not mechanistically. Directions in activation space, including the assistant persona direction, are almost always extracted from English and assumed to generalize across languages. title: Trained on Harm, Still Refusing: A Training-Time Defense for Code Generation
authors: Miaoqing Tian, Ruohan Li, Qian Lu et al.
abstract: Fine-tuning enables safety-aligned code language models to adapt to diverse downstream tasks. However, training on untrusted data can severely undermine their ability to refuse harmful requests. Notably, we find that models comply with harmful requests even though harmfulness information remains highly decodable from their internal representations. title: AMARIS: Merging Generalist and Specialist LLMs via Adaptive Subspace Inheritance
authors: Hwee Young Kang, Irwin De Tao Chin, Wen-Haw Chong et al.
abstract: Domain specialization of large language models (LLMs) often improves target-domain performance but degrades broad capabilities. Model merging is an attractive training-free alternative, yet common parameter-space strategies (for example, interpolation and sparsified averaging) provide limited control over task-specific interference. title: WaXup: Weight Averaging of Experts as Data Augmentation for Robust Introspection
authors: Marc Boëlle, Lucas Dixon, Alexandre Ramé
abstract: As the capabilities of large language models keep improving, traditional mechanistic interpretability methods struggle to keep pace. In contrast, trainable introspection methods emerge as a promising alternative; they repurpose the model itself as a self-diagnostic tool, trained to verbalize what it has learned during finetuning in natural language. title: MAPES: Multi-Value Alignment Pipeline via Expert Specialization
authors: SungHo Kim, SangKeun Lee
abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences requires simultaneously satisfying multiple, often competing values. Existing preference optimization methods collapse these into a single implicit signal, and even multi-objective extensions optimize within a shared parameter space, leaving cross-value conflicts unresolved. title: CENTRY: A Probabilistic Latent-State Model for Continual AI Risk Estimation, Monitoring, and Regulation
authors: Bonny Banerjee, Geetha Raju
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
authors: Andrea Gregor de Varda, Ferdinando D'Elia, Greta Tuckute et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. title: MemOnce: A Scalable Memory Architecture for Large Language Models
authors: Chang Nie, Chaoyou Fu, Songlin Liu et al.
abstract: Deploying large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon and continual interactions requires maintaining reusable memory states for future inference, posing challenges for existing architectures. Standard Transformers accumulate layer-wise, token-level KV caches, incurring linear GPU memory growth and quadratic computational complexity as the context expands. title: DistDNA: Language Model Fingerprinting under Stochastic Decoding
authors: Lifan Hu, Qian Yu, Zhaomin Wu et al.
abstract: Behavioral fingerprints identify a large language model (LLM) from its responses to a shared set of prompts, enabling applications such as verifying whether a deployed model corresponds to the checkpoint it claims to be. Deployed models, however, are commonly served with stochastic decoding, under which the same model may produce different responses to an identical prompt, depending on an unknown temperature and top-$p$ setting. title: Neural Defend ARCAS 290M: A Robust Foundation Model for AI-Generated Audio Detection
authors: Sivashankar Selvarajan, Piyush Verma, Sumit Kumar et al.
abstract: Voice cloning now needs only seconds of audio, and detectors tuned to one dataset often fail when the generator, channel, or language changes. We introduce ARCAS 290M, Neural Defend's foundation model for detecting AI-generated audio. A single frozen production model, with no benchmark-specific fine-tuning, generalizes across text-to-speech, voice-conversion, and codec-language-model generators, telephone and Bluetooth channels, recording conditions, and languages. title: A Benchmark Protocol and Fairness Analysis Towards Open-Set EEG Seizure Type Classification
authors: Targol Bakhtiarvand, Terrance E. Boult, Jugal Kalita et al.
abstract: Automated EEG seizure type classification systems are typically trained and evaluated under the closed-set assumption, where all seizure types encountered at deployment are seen during training. In clinical practice, this assumption fails: patients present with rare or atypical seizure types that fall outside the training label space, and a system that forces a wrong label is worse than one that abstains. title: Enhancing Attention with Higher-Order Attention
authors: R. I. Cukier
abstract: Current decoder large language models rely on a combination of attention, feed forward and residual layers. The attention used is autoregressive (AR) though this is not strictly correct, as we note. That motivates the introduction of other attention methods that, while also not strictly AR, do enhance the AR character. title: Average-Depth Variable Execution via Request-Local Token Routing
authors: Pengjie Zheng, Mengwei Xie, Huan Yang et al.
abstract: Layer skipping can reduce large language model inference costs, but a request budget does not specify how to allocate layer execution across generated tokens. We introduce \method{}, which allows tokens to execute different numbers of layers while matching each request's mean executed depth to a continuous budget. title: AutoOntologyBench: A Task-Grounded Benchmark for Agentic Knowledge Engineering
authors: Minye Shao, Chenghao Xiao, Xingyue Zhao et al.
abstract: Foundation-model agents are increasingly extending beyond software engineering (SWE) into autonomous scientific research, where acquiring and integrating domain knowledge remains a critical challenge. Recent industrial advances have increasingly adopted knowledge graphs and ontology-based semantic layers to organize heterogeneous knowledge into reusable representations. title: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders
authors: Alessandro Piccolo, Francesco De Nicolò, Francesco Manco et al.
abstract: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). title: Auditing Post-Training Unlearning in Diffusion Language Models using Sparse Autoencoders
authors: Yunha Seo, Changhoon Kim
abstract: Machine unlearning is an approach to privacy protection: it aims to remove the influence of designated data while preserving the model's behavior on information that should be retained. While a growing body of work investigates this objective in autoregressive large language models, machine unlearning remains underexplored in diffusion language models (DLMs). title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
authors: Oliver Schön, Adrien Banse, John Lygeros et al.
abstract: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. title: Silent Arbitration: How Large Language Models Resolve Co-Authoritative Conflicting Instructions
authors: Sihyeon Lee, Jiwoo Kum, Jihun Song et al.
abstract: Large language models increasingly receive high-level instructions about roles, values, interests, and communication style. Such instructions can conflict even when a prompt assigns them equal authority and provides no priority rule. We study co-authoritative persona conflict, in which a single prompt jointly assigns two opposing personas. title: No Audio, No Transcripts, No Problem: LLM-based ASR Adaptation Using Only Domain Documents
authors: Sergio Burdisso, Dairazalia Sánchez-Cortés, Esaú Villatoro-Tello et al.
abstract: Can a speech recognizer be adapted to a new domain with no target audio and no transcripts, using only written documentation? This is the realistic onboarding setting: a new customer hands over raw documentation, not the transcripts that text-only adaptation normally assumes. title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations
authors: Davide Gardenal, Mingxuan Liu, Flavio Vella et al.
abstract: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. title: EcomWriteBench: A Real-World Benchmark for E-commerce Writing Tasks
authors: Kaicheng Liang, Jingyi Cui, Hongwei Wen et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used throughout e-commerce workflows to generate content that informs purchasing decisions and supports customer interactions. Evaluating these systems requires accounting for user needs, product evidence, structural constraints, and business requirements that are not fully captured by general-purpose writing benchmarks. We introduce EcomWriteBench, a real-world benchmark containing 3,861 queries from 69 e-commerce writing tasks across 13 categories

title: No Perfect Guardrail & No Perfect Guard: On the Decidability of Output Policies for Large Language Models
authors: Ahmed Amer, Loren Kinczel, Darrell D. E. Long
abstract: Expecting guardrails to provide a general guarantee of safety fails to recognize the limits of computational enforcement and policy specification. We argue that promising such perfection is an ethical failure of precision, and that invoking it to abdicate responsibility is a moral failure. title: Neural Defend Ranks #1 in Global Audio Deepfake Detection Benchmark - ARCAS on the Podonos Independent Leaderboard
authors: Sivashankar Selvarajan, Piyush Verma, Sumit Singh
abstract: Commercial detectors of AI-generated audio are usually promoted with results on internal test sets that buyers cannot inspect. Independent benchmarks with private labels give a more reliable comparison. We report the results of Neural Defend's ARCAS foundation models on the Podonos audio deepfake detection benchmark, an independent leaderboard that scores commercial detection APIs and open-source detectors on one held-out set of real speech and speech from current text-to-speech and voice-clonin

title: A Frugal AI Framework for India: Responsible and Right-sized AI
authors: Balaraman Ravindran, K. S. Venkataraghavan, Gokul S Krishnan et al.
abstract: India's AI debate often swings between two insufficient options: replicating the compute-intensive, capital-heavy foundation-model programmes of the United States or China, or remaining a downstream adopter of foreign AI with localised interfaces and safeguards. Neither serves a country that must deliver AI to a very large, diverse population across uneven infrastructure and within constrained budgets. title: Felid: A Flexible and Efficient Design for Transformer Fine-Tuning over Encrypted Data
authors: Linru Zhang, Jun Jie Sim, Xiangning Wang et al.
abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables non-interactive, privacy-preserving transformer fine-tuning, protecting highly sensitive data as inputs to large language models. Prior work has predominantly pursued efficiency gains through architectural refinements, yet overall performance remains bounded by the substantial cost inherent in encrypted computation. title: When Students Fail to Learn from Teachers: Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation
authors: Xinnan Zhang, Zeyi Liao, Siliang Zeng et al.
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has become a core technique for post-training large language models, enabling students to learn from dense token-level supervision on their own generations. However, even with a capable teacher, OPD training can be unstable, leading to excessive response length, repetitive generation, and severe performance degradation. title: Schema-Validated LLM Workflows: A Benchmark Protocol and Comparative Evaluation Across Six Python Implementations
authors: Sidney Shapiro, Sanad Al-Khatib, Aurora Pinzón Arzola et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to extract records, generate SQL, summarize reports, answer policy questions, and route operational work. At these software boundaries, parseable output is necessary but does not establish task correctness. title: One state, many questions: Opsis gives a frontier model typed eyes for pathology
authors: Zhixuan Ge, Wei Qiu
abstract: A synoptic pathology report is a checklist of questions with fixed answer sets, many composed from others. Pathology foundation models answer them accurately with one classifier trained with labels for each, and frontier language models, which compose freely, cannot fit a slide of fourteen thousand tiles in their context. title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
authors: Faraz Tahmasebi, Michael Pellauer, Hyoukjun Kwon et al.
abstract: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. title: When Do LLM-Elicited Priors Help? A Controlled Audit of Language Models as Priors for Small-Sample Bayesian Regression
authors: Ran Zou, Yang Liu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly asked where to center the coefficients of a small-sample Bayesian regression, but the evidence is unclear: benchmarks are often built to match the prior and models may remember them. We audit this practice with one frontier and one flash-tier model, using hidden feature names, post-cutoff housing data and a pre-specified test that gives features the wrong descriptions. title: Ruby: State-of-the-Art Potency Prediction across Discovery Regimes Using Learned Structural Representations
authors: Michael Atkin, Dominique Beaini, Jules Berman et al.
abstract: Small-molecule drug discovery proceeds through repeated design-make-test-analyze cycles. The goal is often to maximize potency while keeping other properties within the ranges required for a viable therapeutic candidate. Compound prioritization places different demands on computational methods as drug discovery progresses from hit identification through hit-to-lead and lead optimization, with changing computational budgets and increasing amounts of on-target experimental data. title: Self-similar Organization of Information in Language
authors: Leon Lufkin, Cutter Dawes, Kamesh Krishnamurthy
abstract: How much information relevant to predicting the future of a passage (i.e. predictive information) is carried by the preceding text, and how is this information distributed along that history? These questions are fundamental to understanding both the statistical structure of language and what large language models (LLMs) can learn about it. title: Tokenize Moments, Not Frames: Tokenizer-Aware Budget Allocation for Training-Free Video LLM Acceleration
authors: Zirui Zhao, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong
abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Analyzing frame similarity and the vision tokenizers of 16 open models, we trace this loss to a step before token selection. authors: Hao Zhang, Bin Xiao, Kefeng Zhang
abstract: Retrieval-based sparse attention, exemplified by DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), reduces attention computation by selecting a small subset of key-value entries. However, selecting these entries can still require searching the entire visible history. For long sequences, retrieval becomes a major bottleneck, limiting the efficiency gains from sparse attention. title: Beyond Math, Code, and Logic: Do Reasoning Models Transfer to Scientific Argumentation?
authors: Buse Sibel Korkmaz, Antonio del Rio Chanona
abstract: Scientific discourse depends on argumentative reasoning: identifying claims, evaluating evidence, and constructing coherent responses. While recent advances in reasoning-capable language models have demonstrated strong performance on mathematical, coding, and logical benchmarks, their ability to engage in scientific argumentation remains unclear. title: Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and Practical Multilingual Translation Models in the Wild
authors: Mao Zheng, Zheng Li, Fangxu Liu et al.
abstract: Hy-MT3 is the third generation of the Hunyuan multilingual translation model family, including \textbf{Hy-MT3-1.8B}, \textbf{Hy-MT3-7B} and \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B (MoE)}. title: Adapting AI Weather Foundation Models to a Changing Climate
authors: Xinlei Xiong, Wenbo Hu, Shuxun Zhou et al.
abstract: AI weather foundation models learn from historical archives, while the climate distribution encountered during deployment continues to evolve. This growing model--climate mismatch motivates continual adaptation without repeated full-model retraining, but the structure of weather forecast errors determines how such adaptation should be performed. authors: Seunghan Lee, Jun Seo, Junhyeok Kang et al.
abstract: A financial report drafted by an LLM can state every number correctly but still go beyond its input, adding judgments and causes that no one supplied. authors: Joshua Broyde, Sarita A. Joshi
abstract: Deploying generative AI agents in enterprise clinical workflows requires enforcing multi-dimensional safety and compliance policies--preventing HIPAA Protected Health Information (PHI) exposure, maintaining clinical scope-of-practice boundaries, ensuring patient-appropriate reading comprehension, and preserving brand integrity--under interactive latency constraints. title: Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem
authors: Oriol Alàs, Ian Palacín, Iván Cester et al.
abstract: EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of deliverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scattered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate relevant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline.

title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development
authors: Hang Zhang, Yuzhi Pan, Ziyao Zhong et al.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
authors: Mengxiao Wang, Mahbub Alam, Kalyan Nakka et al.
abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. title: Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models
authors: Chang Yang, Yao Xuan, Wendan Yan et al.
abstract: Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher
authors: Guoxin Chen, Shuang Sun, Fanzhe Meng et al.
abstract: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
authors: K. R. Jayaram, Vatche Isahagian, Aswath Vaithinathan Aravindan et al.
abstract: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. title: SkillBridge: Cost-Aware Diagnosis and Repair of Cross-OS Compatibility Defects in Agent Skills
authors: Anjie Xu, Zixing Wang, Yifeng Cai et al.
abstract: LLM agents increasingly reuse executable capabilities through skills, but a skill that works on one OS may fail on another because OS assumptions are spread across guide text, scripts, metadata, install contracts, and local entrypoints. Diagnosing such failures by running every skill on every OS is expensive: many executions spend model tokens, runner time, and review effort before revealing whether the failure is truly OS-related. title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
authors: Zihao Xu, Yuekang Li, Ruitao Feng et al.
abstract: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). authors: Hai Wang, Bretislav Hajek, Chonghe Jiang et al.
abstract: Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it is solved well at scale. title: SheetAlign: Grounded Interaction and Stage-Isolated Learning for Spreadsheet Agents
authors: Yuxiang Wang, Junhao Gan, Jianzhong Qi
abstract: Spreadsheets are widely used for data analysis and supporting decision-making. Automating spreadsheet analysis while protecting sensitive data and controlling deployment costs motivates locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs). title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations
authors: Alexandra Starostina, Alexander Hermann, Mahish Guru et al.
abstract: Simulation-driven design of real engineering components has to meet three conditions at once. title: Verifiable Logic in Medical LLMs: A Critical Review of Agentic Clinical Reasoning Optimization and Neuro-Symbolic Grounding
authors: Youssef ElNahas, Adel Ammar, Soumaya Chaffar et al.
abstract: Clinical large language models are usually judged by whether the final answer is right. Yet a model can reach a fluent, plausible output through invalid reasoning that static benchmarks do not detect, and confident hallucination, causally invalid inference, and spurious demographic shortcuts can pass conventional evaluation. authors: Xinzhuang Xiong, Yonghao Wang, Shengyao Sun et al.
abstract: Large language models enable agents to optimize RTL using EDA feedback, yet their executable search procedures remain largely hand- engineered.
